copy.intro: You will meet these claims in videos, comments and books. Some come from people who believe the Shroud is real, some from people who are sure it is a fake. We checked each one. Where the case file already covers it, we link to the full exhibit. Where it does not, the sources are right here.
copy.filterLabel: Filter by who usually says it
copy.verdictKey: What the labels mean: False means the record shows the opposite. No evidence means nothing supports it. Unproven means it is possible but not shown. Overstated means something real has been stretched. Partly true means the fact is right but the conclusion drawn from it is not.
copy.seeExhibit: Full exhibit in the case file:

items.claim: The carbon dating has been debunked.
items.check: The 1988 test has real weak points. All samples came from one corner, and when the raw data were released, reanalyses found the measurements do not agree with each other as well as the published result implied. But no laboratory has produced a new date, and no reanalysis has moved the result to the first century. Criticizing a test is not the same as overturning it. The 1988 date is still the strongest evidence against authenticity.

items.claim: The samples were switched, or the result was rigged.
items.check: Some writers accused the laboratories or the organizers of swapping the Shroud samples for medieval cloth. No evidence of a swap has ever been produced. The cutting was filmed and witnessed, and each laboratory also dated control cloths of known age and got those dates right.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Radiocarbon dating of the Shroud of Turin

items.claim: The labs dated an invisible medieval repair.
items.check: Chemist Raymond Rogers reported that threads from the dated corner differ from the main cloth. Others examined a leftover piece of the 1988 sample and found no sign of a repair. Possible, not shown.

items.claim: The 1532 fire, bacteria or a burst of neutrons changed the date.
items.check: Each idea has been proposed and none has been shown. To make a first-century cloth test as medieval, a large share of the carbon in the sample, roughly a third or more, would have to be later contamination that survived the lab cleaning. No one has found it.

items.claim: New scientific methods dated it to the time of Christ.
items.check: Two newer methods, X-ray scattering on one thread and Fanti's fiber tests, gave results compatible with the first century. Neither method has been tested on many cloths of known age, and both depend on assumptions. Promising, not a date.

items.claim: You can see coins over the eyes, writing and flowers in the image.
items.check: These shapes show up only in heavily processed photographs, and other researchers looking at the same images do not see them. The human eye easily finds patterns in noise. We do not count them as evidence.

items.claim: Pollen proves the cloth was in Jerusalem.
items.check: The pollen came from sticky tape samples taken in the 1970s. A later pollen expert concluded the grains cannot be identified down to the plant species, so the Jerusalem conclusion should be set aside until new samples are studied. That has not happened yet.

items.claim: The blood is type AB, the same as other famous relics.
items.check: Typing very old, degraded blood is unreliable, and AB is a known false result with aged samples. The evidence that the stains are blood is good. The blood type is not settled.

items.claim: The Sudarium of Oviedo confirms it.
items.check: The Sudarium is a face cloth kept in Oviedo, Spain. Matching its stains to the Shroud is a matter of interpretation, and radiocarbon tests on the Sudarium itself gave dates around the 7th century. It cannot add weight to the Shroud.

items.claim: The Church has declared it authentic.
items.check: The Catholic Church has never ruled that it is authentic. In 1998 Pope John Paul II said the Church has no specific competence to decide the question and leaves it to science. Popes call it an icon. Allowing veneration is not a verdict.

items.claim: NASA proved the image is 3D.
items.check: The 3D effect is real and is in the case file. But it was found in 1976 by two U.S. Air Force scientists, John Jackson and Eric Jumper, using a VP-8 Image Analyzer. It was not a NASA study, although some members of the later 1978 team worked at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. The 3D effect shows the image relates to distance from a body. It does not show how the image was made.

items.claim: Scientists say it took 34 trillion watts of light to make the image.
items.check: The number comes from Italian laser experiments (ENEA, 2011) that colored small pieces of linen with ultraviolet pulses. The researchers estimated the power their method would need for a whole body image and noted no light source today can deliver it. That is an estimate about their own method. It is not a measurement taken from the Shroud, and it is not evidence of a resurrection.

sources.label: Di Lazzaro et al. 2011, ENEA report RT/2011/14 (Italian)

items.claim: Leonardo da Vinci made it.
items.check: The cloth was already on display in Lirey, France, in the 1350s, and a pilgrim badge from that time still survives. Leonardo was born in 1452, about a century later.

sources.label: Lirey pilgrim badge, Musée de Cluny
Wikipedia: History of the Shroud of Turin

items.claim: The forger confessed in the Middle Ages.
items.check: A real letter from Bishop Pierre d'Arcis in 1389 says an earlier bishop found the artist who painted it. This is serious evidence and it is in the case file. But the artist is never named and no record of that earlier inquiry has been found. It is a report of a confession, not a confession we can read.

items.claim: It is just a painting. Paint was found on it.
items.check: Walter McCrone found tiny paint particles and concluded it was painted. The 1978 team found that the image itself has no pigment, binder or brush marks, and that scattered particles likely came from painted copies pressed against it over the centuries. Paint particles are on the cloth. The image is not made of them.

items.claim: Scientists have made a perfect copy.
items.check: Several copies come close in a photograph, the best known by Luigi Garlaschelli in 2009. Up close each one differs. In his copy the color sits in pigment, not only in the thin top layer of the fibers. Every copy so far matches some features, and none matches all of them.

items.claim: It is a medieval photograph.
items.check: Some writers proposed that someone in the Middle Ages used a camera obscura and light-sensitive chemicals, and a modern researcher made a similar image with a quartz lens and silver salts. But the 1978 X-ray fluorescence tests found no silver or other photographic chemicals in the image area, and there is no record of such technology at the time.

items.claim: It is a scorch from a heated statue.
items.check: Scorches on linen glow under ultraviolet light. The burns from the 1532 fire on the Shroud do glow. The body image does not. That makes a simple scorch unlikely.

items.claim: The Gospels say Jesus was wrapped in strips, not one sheet.
items.check: Mark, Matthew and Luke use sindon, a linen sheet. John uses othonia, a plural word for linen cloths, and mentions a separate face cloth. The words can fit one large sheet plus smaller cloths. The Gospels neither prove nor rule out the Shroud.

items.claim: There were many 'shrouds of Jesus', so this is just one more.
items.check: True, medieval Europe had several cloths claimed as Jesus's burial cloths. The one at Cadouin in France turned out to be an Egyptian fabric from around 1100, with an Arabic inscription naming a caliph. But none of them carries an image like this one. Many fakes tell us to be careful. They do not tell us that this one is fake.

sources.label: The Cloth of Cadouin, Shroud Spectrum International 18

items.claim: The Church admitted it is a fake.
items.check: No pope or Church body has declared it a fake, just as none has declared it authentic. In 1390 a pope at Avignon allowed it to be shown only as a representation, and today popes call it an icon. Both leave the question of its origin open.

items.claim: Jesus never existed, so it cannot be his.
items.check: Almost all historians of the period, including skeptics, agree that Jesus of Nazareth lived and was crucified under Pontius Pilate. The Roman historian Tacitus mentions his execution around the year 116. Whether this cloth is his is a separate question, and that question is what this site is about.
